paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork asks an agent to cooperate with teammates it has not encountered before. Training for this situation commonly depends on interacting with an environment and having carefully designed teammates available. This paper studies an offline alternative: learning the focal agent’s policy directly from recorded interactions among multiple agents.

The proposed framework, TAGET, uses hierarchical sequence modeling to address limited training data, incomplete observations, and adaptation during use. Its central mechanism predicts both teammate-aware rewards-to-go and sub-goals dynamically. These predictions describe anticipated future reward and intermediate objectives while accounting for teammates, giving the agent a way to adjust as their behavior changes.

The experiments report substantial improvements over existing ad hoc teamwork approaches in the offline setting. The contribution is therefore a way to connect training from fixed records with responsive collaboration at deployment. Offline learning describes how the policy is acquired; TAGET’s changing predictions provide the mechanism for adapting its behavior when working with unfamiliar teammates.
icml-2025-ad-hoc-teamwork-via-offline-go.tldr: TAGET learns teamwork from recorded interactions and dynamically predicts teammate-aware goals and future rewards to adapt to unfamiliar collaborators.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical account of what many representation learning methods learn. Its starting point is the association between an input and a context variable. The authors show that methods across supervised, self-supervised, and manifold learning can be examined through this relationship, despite their different training setups.

The theory describes many methods as approximating the leading singular functions of an expectation operator defined by the context. These functions characterize prominent patterns in the input–context relationship; a representation that captures them is said to learn the contexture. The authors prove optimality for tasks compatible with that context, making the relationship between training context and downstream task central to the guarantee.

A consequence is that increasing model size yields diminishing returns once the relevant functions can be approximated adequately. Within this account, further improvement requires better contexts. The paper also proposes a way to assess context quality without knowing the downstream tasks and reports that its metric correlates well with encoder performance across many real datasets.
icml-2025-contextures-representations-fr.tldr: Contexture theory connects many representation learning methods through their training contexts and explains when better contexts matter more than larger models.

paragraphs: Image anomaly detection identifies regions that differ from normal examples. Existing methods often reconstruct a normal version of an image or compare learned features with normal samples. Both approaches rely on matching, and inaccurate matches can distort the resulting anomaly scores. CostFilter-AD targets this intermediate source of error.

The method first builds a matching cost volume: a structure with two image-location dimensions and another dimension representing possible matches. A filtering network then refines these costs. It uses the input image as an attention query across multiple feature layers, aiming to suppress matching noise while retaining boundaries and detecting small or subtle abnormalities.

CostFilter-AD is designed as a post-processing component that can be added to either reconstruction-based or embedding-based detectors. Experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA report benefits for both single-class and multi-class detection. The stated findings support improving the reliability of the matching stage as a useful route to better anomaly localization, with applicability across both major detector families.
icml-2025-costfilter-ad-enhancing-anomal.tldr: CostFilter-AD improves image anomaly detection by filtering noisy matching costs while preserving boundaries and subtle abnormalities.

paragraphs: CUPS estimates sequences of three-dimensional human poses and body shapes from RGB video while also learning uncertainty about those estimates. During training, it generates and scores multiple hypotheses. This makes uncertainty part of the learning process and produces an uncertainty function trained jointly with the pose estimator.

After training, that function supplies a conformity score for calibrating a conformal predictor. The score connects the model’s learned assessment of uncertainty to a procedure for assessing prediction quality. The method therefore uses uncertainty in two linked roles: helping train the estimator and supporting calibrated assessment of its outputs.

A central complication is that human pose and shape data are not fully exchangeable, an assumption relevant to conformal prediction guarantees. The authors address this by providing two practical bounds on the coverage gap. They report state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and datasets alongside probabilistic guarantees, with those coverage-gap bounds providing theoretical backing for the treatment of uncertainty in this setting.
icml-2025-cups-improving-human-pose-shap.tldr: CUPS jointly learns human pose estimates and uncertainty, then uses conformal calibration with coverage-gap bounds for data that are not fully exchangeable.

paragraphs: Two optimization formulations can express the same problem using different variables or constraints. Recognizing this equivalence matters when systems generate formulations from natural-language descriptions, because surface differences can make simple checks unreliable. This paper introduces a formal criterion and an automated framework for examining such relationships.

The criterion, Quasi-Karp equivalence, is based on the existence of a mapping between the formulations’ decision variables. EquivaMap uses a language model to discover candidate mappings, followed by verification that mapped solutions preserve feasibility and optimality. That verification stage operates without additional solver calls, connecting the model’s proposed correspondence to the properties that make the formulations equivalent.

The authors also construct EquivaFormulation, an open dataset built by transforming existing formulations through operations such as adding slack variables or valid inequalities. Their experiments report substantially better equivalence identification than existing methods. The contribution combines a defined notion of equivalence, automated mapping discovery, and verification, providing a more structured basis for checking generated optimization formulations.
icml-2025-equivamap-leveraging-llms-for-.tldr: EquivaMap uses language models to discover variable mappings and verifies whether they establish equivalence between optimization formulations.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a common mathematical language for problems in engineering, economics, and machine learning, but their flexibility can make them computationally difficult. This paper introduces expected variational inequalities, which change the object being sought: the goal is a distribution satisfying the inequality constraint in expectation.

That relaxation is the key to the computational result. By adapting techniques from game theory, the authors show that expected variational inequalities can be solved in polynomial time for general, nonmonotone operators. The guarantee concerns the expected constraint under the resulting distribution; it does not assert that each individual outcome separately solves the original variational inequality.

The framework includes correlated equilibria, an established game-theoretic solution concept, while extending beyond games. It also brings together and generalizes results involving smooth games, shared constraints, and nonconcave utilities. Its significance is both computational and conceptual: changing the solution requirement to an expectation makes a broad relaxation tractable and places several previously separate results within one framework.
icml-2025-expected-variational-inequalit.tldr: Expected variational inequalities relax constraints to hold under a distribution’s expectation, enabling polynomial-time solutions even for general nonmonotone operators.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained model to understand three-dimensional point clouds can require substantial storage and can erode previously learned knowledge. Parameter-efficient transfer methods reduce the amount of training, but the authors’ analysis finds that existing 3D methods inadequately align feature relationships with the semantic needs of downstream tasks.

Their approach brings in semantic information from frozen pretrained 2D models. These models provide vision semantic prompts, which a Hybrid Attention Adapter combines with the 3D representations. The resulting adaptation uses 1.8 million trainable parameters. The central idea is to make the limited trainable component more informative by supplying semantic cues already available in another visual representation.

Experiments cover ScanObjectNN, ModelNet40, and ShapeNetPart. The method achieves 95.6% accuracy on ModelNet40 and reported performance of 90.09% on ScanObjectNN’s challenging PB-T50-RS classification split. These findings support the proposed combination of parameter-efficient adaptation and 2D semantic guidance for point-cloud understanding, showing that a relatively small adaptation module can make useful use of frozen visual knowledge.
icml-2025-exploring-vision-semantic-prom.tldr: Frozen 2D visual models supply semantic prompts that a compact attention adapter integrates into pretrained 3D point-cloud representations.

paragraphs: Full attention is a major computational bottleneck in video diffusion Transformers. The paper gives an example where attention consumes 800 of 950 seconds needed to generate a five-second 720P video. Its starting observation is that attention in pretrained video diffusion models concentrates mainly within local regions of space and time.

Sliding tile attention, or STA, exploits that locality by moving attention windows over spatial-temporal regions. It organizes computation tile by tile with a hardware-aware design. This organization matters because restricting attention mathematically is only part of the problem: the resulting operations also need to execute efficiently on the hardware.

With kernel optimizations, STA reports 58.79% model FLOPs utilization and a 7.17-fold speed advantage over prior implementations. On Hunyuan, attention runs 1.6–10 times faster than FlashAttention-3, translating into 1.36–3.53 times faster overall generation with no or minimal quality loss. The distinction between attention speed and total generation speed shows how improvements to a dominant component carry through to the complete system.
icml-2025-fast-video-generation-with-sli.tldr: Sliding tile attention combines local spatial-temporal attention with hardware-aware computation to accelerate video generation with no or minimal reported quality loss.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning must learn from recorded experience without real-time environmental feedback. This makes unfamiliar states and actions difficult to assess. The paper argues that diffusion approaches centered on each agent’s history miss important coordination relationships, weakening collaborative behavior when the environment changes.

MCGD represents those relationships using a sparse coordination graph with continuous node attributes and discrete edge attributes. It derives transition probabilities between edge categories and uses adaptive categorical diffusion to model different coordination structures. This gives the method an explicit representation of how interactions among agents can vary.

The graph also shapes action generation: forward noise depends on neighboring agents, and anisotropic diffusion increases each agent’s action diversity. Thus, coordination structure influences the diffusion process itself. Experiments across multiple environments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in coordination performance and robustness under dynamic conditions. The findings support modeling variation in both interaction structure and individual actions as a useful combination for offline collaborative policies.
icml-2025-graph-diffusion-for-robust-mul.tldr: MCGD uses graph-structured diffusion to model changing coordination relationships and improve the performance and robustness of offline multi-agent policies.

paragraphs: Image-caption collections scraped from the web can contain incorrect descriptions, creating unreliable training material for vision-language models. A common filtering signal is the similarity between an image’s representation and its caption’s representation. LEMoN broadens the evidence used to judge a pair by considering its multimodal neighborhood.

The method operates in the latent space of a contrastively pretrained multimodal model, where images and captions have learned representations. It uses neighboring image-caption pairs to identify likely labeling errors automatically. The authors provide both theoretical justification and empirical validation for using this surrounding structure as evidence about whether a caption is appropriate.

Across eight datasets and twelve baselines, LEMoN improves label-error detection by more than 3%. Training on data filtered with LEMoN also improves downstream captioning by over two BLEU points compared with noisy training. These results connect the filtering method to two outcomes: detecting incorrect pairs and improving a model trained on the cleaned data. The downstream result makes the practical value of better error detection explicit.
icml-2025-lemon-label-error-detection-us.tldr: LEMoN detects incorrect image captions using nearby multimodal representations, with reported gains in both label-error detection and downstream captioning.

paragraphs: Choosing a language model for a particular task is expensive when every candidate must be fine-tuned before comparison. LensLLM approaches selection by modeling how models behave during fine-tuning and using that information to predict their downstream performance. The goal is to make selection both accurate and computationally economical.

The theoretical foundation is a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound that characterizes fine-tuning dynamics. Building on that analysis, the authors introduce a rectified scaling model based on the Neural Tangent Kernel. This provides a predictive model of performance across tasks, linking the theory of adaptation to the practical decision of which language model to use.

On three large-scale benchmarks, the paper reports selection accuracy of up to 91.1% and computational cost reductions of up to 88.5%, outperforming five state-of-the-art methods. These are reported maxima across the evaluated settings. The findings support the value of modeling adaptation dynamics when comparing candidate models, allowing selection to benefit from predictions about fine-tuning without paying the full cost of fine-tuning every candidate.
icml-2025-lensllm-unveiling-fine-tuning-.tldr: LensLLM models fine-tuning dynamics to predict which language models will perform well on downstream tasks while reducing model-selection costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the agent receives only the accumulated reward for an entire trajectory. Such feedback is useful when obtaining a separate reward at every step is prohibitively expensive. The challenge is to learn effective behavior from an overall outcome without directly observing each step’s reward contribution.

For a finite-horizon Markov decision process with S states, A actions, horizon H, and K episodes, the authors develop an algorithm with asymptotically nearly optimal regret of order sqrt(SAH³K), up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures cumulative performance lost relative to optimal behavior. The result describes how this learning cost scales with the problem size and the number of episodes.

Two technical ingredients support the bound. The algorithm uses ideas from linear bandits to construct a tighter confidence region for the reward function, and it builds a reference transition model to guide exploration. Together, these address uncertainty about rewards and decisions about where to explore, yielding a near-optimal theoretical guarantee despite receiving only trajectory-level reward feedback.
icml-2025-minimax-optimal-regret-bound-f.tldr: A new algorithm achieves asymptotically nearly optimal regret when reinforcement learning receives only total rewards for complete trajectories.

paragraphs: Learning properties of graphs, such as molecular solubility, can make training graph convolutional networks expensive. GraNT treats training-example selection as a teaching problem. From a dense collection of graph-property pairs representing an implicit mapping, a teacher chooses a subset intended to help the learner converge faster.

The paper supplies a theoretical connection between this teaching view and ordinary network training. It analyzes how graph structure affects parameter-based gradient descent, then describes the network’s evolution through functional gradient descent in a nonparametric teaching framework. The resulting analysis establishes consistency between teaching graph convolutional networks and teaching learners that account for graph structure through their implicit mappings.

Experiments report training-time reductions of 36.62% for graph regression, 38.19% for graph classification, 30.97% for node regression, and 47.30% for node classification, while maintaining generalization performance. These findings connect the theoretical teaching perspective to practical savings across several prediction settings. The contribution centers on selecting informative training examples to improve learning efficiency without sacrificing the reported ability to generalize.
icml-2025-nonparametric-teaching-for-gra.tldr: GraNT uses a theoretically grounded teaching strategy to select graph examples and reduce training time while maintaining generalization performance.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows model probabilities for continuous data and can also generate samples. This paper revisits their capabilities through TarFlow, a scalable architecture that directly models and generates image pixels. The work asks how far a standalone flow model can go with a modern architecture and techniques aimed at sample quality.

TarFlow uses a stack of autoregressive Transformer blocks operating on image patches, with the autoregressive direction alternating between layers. It is trained end to end. Three additional techniques improve generation: Gaussian noise augmentation during training, denoising after training, and guidance that works in both class-conditional and unconditional settings.

The combined system reports new state-of-the-art image likelihood estimates, exceeding previous methods by a large margin. It also produces samples whose quality and diversity are comparable to diffusion models. These findings address both probability modeling and generation, supporting the claim that normalizing flows have greater practical capability than previously recognized. The reported comparison is achieved with a standalone normalizing-flow model equipped with the proposed architecture and sampling improvements.
icml-2025-normalizing-flows-are-capable-.tldr: TarFlow combines autoregressive Transformers with sample-quality improvements to achieve strong image likelihoods and generation comparable to diffusion models.

paragraphs: Updating a language model with new information while preserving its performance is a difficult knowledge-management problem. This paper proposes an attached memory system, using a CPU-and-RAM analogy: the language model processes information, while a peripheral component stores and supplies knowledge. The framework focuses on supporting longer-term knowledge updates.

Memory is organized as a sequence of banks, each modeled with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network to support smooth state transitions. Query signals derived from the language model’s internal states dynamically control reading and writing. This makes access to the memory depend on what the model is currently processing.

A dedicated bank produces a mask indicating the relevance of retrieved information, and the retrieved memory feature is integrated as a prefix to aid prediction. Experiments on knowledge-based model editing report that this design is effective and efficient. The contribution brings storage, adaptive access, and relevance assessment into one memory augmentation mechanism, with the reported evidence showing its utility for editing the knowledge available to a language model.
icml-2025-peripheral-memory-for-llms-int.tldr: Sequential memory banks let a language model dynamically read, write, and assess retrieved knowledge for effective model editing.

paragraphs: Tensor completion reconstructs missing entries in multidimensional data using structure in the entries that are available. This paper focuses on tensors with low multilinear rank. It exploits the geometric structure of the set of tensors with a fixed multilinear rank to design a more effective optimization procedure.

The proposed Preconditioned Riemannian Gradient Descent algorithm, or PRGD, introduces a preconditioned metric on that space. The metric changes the geometry used to guide gradient updates. Compared with standard Riemannian Gradient Descent, PRGD converges faster while retaining the same order of computational complexity per iteration, so its stated advantage does not require a higher asymptotic cost for each update.

The authors provide a recovery guarantee under near-optimal sampling complexity, connecting successful reconstruction to the amount of observed data. Numerical experiments on synthetic tensors and real video inpainting report better efficiency than state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical findings support adapting the optimization geometry as a way to improve low-rank tensor reconstruction.
icml-2025-preconditioned-riemannian-grad.tldr: PRGD changes the optimization geometry for low-rank tensor completion to improve convergence while retaining the same per-iteration complexity order.

paragraphs: Mathematical reasoning from diagrams depends on accurately recognizing fine visual details. This paper identifies visual grounding as a major bottleneck in multimodal language models, despite efforts to expand instruction data and strengthen language backbones. In the authors’ evaluation, GPT-4o has a 70% grounding error rate, and correcting those errors improves reasoning accuracy by 12%.

The proposed approach combines a geometrically grounded vision encoder with a feature router that dynamically selects among hierarchical visual feature maps. Its purpose is to recognize visual primitives accurately and provide precise visual prompts suited to the language model’s reasoning needs. This directly targets the visual information supplied to the reasoning process.

In experiments, PRIMITIVE-Qwen2.5-7B exceeds other 7B models by 12% on MathVerse and performs on par with GPT-4V on MathVista. The findings connect improved fine-grained visual processing with stronger diagram-based mathematical performance. They support investing in how diagram structure is encoded and passed to the language model as an important part of improving multimodal mathematical reasoning.
icml-2025-primitive-vision-improving-dia.tldr: Primitive Vision improves mathematical diagram understanding through geometry-aware visual encoding and dynamic selection of features for language-model reasoning.

paragraphs: Guiding language models with human values can require substantial expert effort when instructions must fit a particular context. Fixed sets of principles offer reusable guidance, but their generality can make them difficult to adapt to individual queries. SPRI addresses this by automatically generating principles for each input in real time.

The generated principles then guide the corresponding response. The framework is designed to require minimal or no human effort, making context-specific guidance part of the model’s workflow. Its central contribution is the creation of principles situated in the immediate task, so that the guidance can reflect the requirements of an individual instance.

The paper evaluates three uses. In a complex domain-specific task, generated principles yield performance comparable to expert-written ones. Instance-specific evaluation rubrics outperform prior language-model judging frameworks, and using SPRI to create synthetic supervised fine-tuning data substantially improves truthfulness. These results show benefits across response guidance, evaluation, and training-data generation in the studied tasks, supporting automated contextual principles as a useful alignment mechanism.
icml-2025-spri-aligning-large-language-m.tldr: SPRI generates principles tailored to each query, with reported benefits for expert-level guidance, response evaluation, and truthfulness training.

paragraphs: Translating everyday questions into SQL requires understanding both what a user wants and how the database is organized. Language models can struggle with those connections. Breaking the task into smaller pieces is also difficult because SQL’s declarative syntax links query concepts to database elements in intricate ways.

SGU-SQL uses query structure to organize this process. It first establishes structure-aware links between the user’s request and the database schema. It then recursively decomposes generation through syntax-based prompting, guiding the language model to build the target SQL incrementally. The decomposition is therefore tied to the language being generated and the database it must reference.

Experiments on two benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art text-to-SQL baselines. The findings support combining schema linkage with syntactic decomposition to help models construct complex queries. The approach makes structural relationships an explicit part of prompting, providing a route from the user’s intended question to the connected pieces needed in a complete SQL statement.
icml-2025-structure-guided-large-languag.tldr: SGU-SQL links user questions to database structure and uses syntax-guided decomposition to build SQL queries incrementally.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine learning across data silos whose distributions can differ substantially. Discrete representations have helped with smaller shifts, but can struggle when a new silo contains unfamiliar data. This paper identifies increased model uncertainty on unfamiliar distributions and uses that observation to decide when the representation should expand.

UEFL maps latent features to trainable discrete vectors stored in a codebook. Its iterative procedure assesses uncertainty and extends that codebook specifically for silos showing high uncertainty. The representation can therefore acquire additional discrete vectors where the existing dictionary appears inadequate for the local distribution.

The framework aims to improve accuracy and reduce uncertainty with minimal computational overhead. Across multiple datasets, the authors report accuracy improvements of 3%–22.1% and uncertainty reductions of 38.83%–96.24% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support uncertainty as a practical signal for targeted codebook growth in heterogeneous federated settings. The reported ranges describe the evaluated settings, showing how adaptive discrete representations can help accommodate substantial differences among silos.
icml-2025-uncertainty-based-extensible-c.tldr: UEFL expands discrete representation codebooks for high-uncertainty data silos, improving reported federated-learning accuracy and reducing uncertainty.

paragraphs: Mechanical metamaterial design involves the relationship among a material’s three-dimensional topology, its density condition, and its mechanical properties. The paper’s literature review finds that most existing models handle only two of these modalities at a time. Complex applications motivate a model that can account for all three together.

UniMate combines a modality alignment module with a synergetic diffusion generation module. This unified design supports topology generation, property prediction, and condition confirmation within the same model. The approach treats the connections among the three modalities as part of a shared modeling problem, reflecting the different kinds of information involved in material design.

Experiments report improvements over baseline models of up to 80.2% for topology generation, 5.1% for property prediction, and 50.2% for condition confirmation. These are task-specific maximum improvements reported by the authors. The findings support the usefulness of jointly modeling the three modalities across multiple design tasks, extending the scope beyond models organized around a single pair of material descriptions.
icml-2025-unimate-a-unified-model-for-me.tldr: UniMate jointly models topology, density conditions, and mechanical properties to support three mechanical metamaterial design tasks.

paragraphs: Process reward models assess reasoning processes and can help language models benefit from additional computation when answering questions. Their training has largely centered on mathematics. This paper first examines transfer beyond that area and finds that current process reward models perform poorly in other domains, motivating broader training data.

VersaPRM is trained on synthetic reasoning data spanning multiple domains, produced through a new generation and annotation method. The contribution links the construction of that data to a process reward model intended for more varied reasoning tasks. The reported evaluations show consistent gains across diverse domains.

One example comes from the Law category of MMLU-Pro. With weighted majority voting, VersaPRM achieves a 7.9% performance gain over ordinary majority voting, compared with a 1.3% gain from Qwen2.5-Math-PRM. This comparison illustrates how a model trained for broader reasoning can provide more useful weighting outside mathematics in the tested setting. The authors also release the data, code, and models, making the synthetic-data approach available for further use.
icml-2025-versaprm-multi-domain-process-.tldr: VersaPRM uses synthetic reasoning data from multiple domains to improve process-based answer evaluation beyond mathematics.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when diffusion generation returns training examples and when it reaches more general points on the data manifold. The analysis uses a simplified setting: shallow ReLU denoisers trained with minimum squared parameter norm. This setting allows the authors to study how the learned model’s bias shapes probability-flow trajectories.

For orthogonal datasets, they introduce a simpler score flow and show that it follows trajectories similar to probability flow, converging to a training point or a sum of training points. Stopping probability flow early through the diffusion time scheduler can instead reach more general manifold points. The analysis therefore connects the timing of generation to memorization and combinations of training examples.

The authors extend their results to obtuse simplex data and run simulations in the orthogonal setting that confirm the described outcomes. They also observe reduced memorization as the number of training samples grows, with fewer generated samples accumulating near training points. These findings characterize behavior under the studied network and data assumptions, giving a theoretical account of both memorization and generation beyond individual examples.
icml-2025-when-diffusion-models-memorize.tldr: In simplified minimum-norm denoisers, probability flow can converge to training examples or their combinations, while early stopping can reach more general manifold points.

paragraphs: A world model captures the underlying process that produces observed data. This paper asks when neural networks can recover the hidden variables of such a process while learning tasks built from them. It gives theoretical results for a multi-task setting, where the same latent variables underlie multiple prediction problems.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that models with a low-degree bias recover those latent variables even when the proxy tasks are complex nonlinear functions of them. The recovery depends on model architecture. Thus, the guarantee identifies a combination of task structure and model bias that supports learning hidden generating factors, with architectural sensitivity remaining part of the result.

The analysis represents Boolean task solutions using the Fourier-Walsh transform and develops techniques for studying invertible Boolean transformations. The paper also illustrates algorithmic implications and connects the theory to self-supervised learning, out-of-distribution generalization, and linear representations in language models. Its contribution is a conditional mathematical account of latent recovery that helps specify when learning several tasks can produce a representation of their shared underlying world.
icml-2025-when-do-neural-networks-learn-.tldr: The paper proves latent-variable recovery in a multi-task setting for models with a low-degree bias under stated assumptions, with results sensitive to architecture.

paragraphs: Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning encourages randomness in an agent’s policy alongside reward seeking. That encouragement can improve exploration and robustness, helping learning across many tasks. This paper examines a tension that arises in demanding control problems: successful behavior may require highly precise actions and a policy with little randomness.

The authors analyze how the balance between robustness and optimality affects policy optimization. Their central finding is that maximizing entropy can steer optimization in an unhelpful direction when the task requires a low-entropy policy. In these cases, the same mechanism that supports exploration can contribute to learning failure, including problems where algorithms without entropy maximization succeed.

Experiments across a variety of control problems demonstrate this misleading effect. The implication is conditional on the control demands and optimization trade-off: entropy encouragement is useful in many settings, but can conflict with the precision needed in others. The analysis offers a clearer basis for balancing reward design and entropy maximization when applying these methods to challenging control tasks.
icml-2025-when-maximum-entropy-misleads-.tldr: Entropy maximization can misdirect reinforcement learning in control tasks that require precise, low-randomness policies.
